summary: A country on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, formerly the site of the Kingdom of Dahomey and the birthplace of Vodun, which became independent from France in 1960.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: From the 15th and 16th centuries Islam entered northern Benin along the trans-Saharan trade routes via Hausa, Fulani and Songhai merchants, and in the 19th century the Fulani jihad movements expanded its influence further. In the south Islam was brought by Yoruba Muslims and by the 'Agudas', freed slaves who returned from Brazil in the 19th century, and Porto-Novo still has a Brazilian-style mosque. In recent years, thanks to population growth in the north and conversions, Muslims have become the largest religious group.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism reached Ouidah in 1861 with missionaries of the Society of African Missions of Lyon, and expanded after France colonized Dahomey in 1894. The French colonial authorities trained civil servants and an intellectual elite in the south through Catholic schools, so Catholicism is especially prevalent in the coastal Fon and Gun areas. Both Pope John Paul II in 1993 and Pope Benedict XVI in 2011 visited Benin.

ranking.name: Other Christians (Celestial Church of Christ, Methodists, Pentecostals, etc.)
ranking.description: This category includes the Methodists (introduced by British missionaries from Lagos in the 19th century), Pentecostals, and the 'Celestial Church of Christ', founded in 1947 by the Beninese Samuel Oschoffa. The Celestial Church of Christ blends Christianity with West African traditional elements, emphasizes visions and charismatic healing, and has many followers in Benin and Nigeria, reflecting the development of indigenized African Christianity.

ranking.name: Vodun
ranking.description: Vodun originated in the traditions of the Fon and Ewe peoples of the south, worshipping ancestral spirits and nature spirits (vodun), and in the Kingdom of Dahomey of the 17th to 19th centuries it was part of the state religion. During the slave trade it spread to Haiti and the Americas with the Africans who were sold. Since 1996 Benin has designated 10 January as the national Vodun Day, Ouidah is an important holy place of Vodun, and many Christians and Muslims also take part in Vodun rituals at the same time.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The share of the non-religious population is not high, and consists mainly of educated city residents. Benin was under the Marxist-Leninist regime of Kérékou from 1974 to 1990, and the government once suppressed traditional religion and the churches, but religion has always been important in people's lives, so only about 6 percent identify as having no religion.

ranking.name: Other traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Other traditional beliefs include the ancestral spirit and land worship of peoples such as the Bariba and Somba in the north, and secret societies and divination traditions in various places, such as the Ifá divination of the Yoruba. These beliefs often coexist with Christianity and Islam, and people consult them at the same time in marriage and funeral rites.

religion.background: From the 17th century the Kingdom of Dahomey in southern Benin, centered on its capital Abomey, had Vodun and royal ancestor worship at the core of its state ideology; the kingdom took part in the Atlantic slave trade, which carried Vodun to Haiti and Brazil. The north, because of the trans-Saharan trade, had contact with Islam earlier. In the mid-19th century Catholic missionaries arrived at Ouidah, and after France conquered Dahomey in 1894, Christianity expanded with colonial education. The Marxist-Leninist regime of 1974-1990 suppressed religion, and after democratization in 1990 religious freedom was restored and Vodun also gained official recognition.

ranking.name: Fon
ranking.description: Fon is the language of the Fon people of the south and belongs to the Gbe branch; the Kingdom of Dahomey (about 1600-1894) had the Fon as its ruling people, making Fon the dominant language of the south. Today it is the most commonly used market and everyday language around the capital Cotonou and the economic center, about one quarter of the population speak it as a mother tongue, and many other peoples also use it as a lingua franca.

ranking.name: Yoruba
ranking.description: Yoruba is spoken mainly in the southeast around Porto-Novo, bordering Nigeria, and in the central region; the Yoruba of Benin (also called Nago) belong to the same people as the Yoruba of Nigeria. During the colonial period Britain and France drew the border and divided the Yoruba area between the two countries, so Yoruba became a cross-border language, accounting for a little over one tenth of Benin's population.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French arrived with the French conquest of Dahomey in 1894, was the language of administration and education during the colonial period, and was made the sole official language after independence in 1960. Because French is learned only at school, very few people have French as a mother tongue, but educated city residents generally speak it, and it is an important language of government, the media and communication between ethnic groups.

language.history: There are more than fifty indigenous languages in Benin; in the south Gbe and Yoruba-family languages such as Fon, Yoruba and Aja predominate, while in the north there are Bariba, Ditammari, Fula and others. The Kingdom of Dahomey of the 17th to 19th centuries made Fon dominant in the south, and during the slave trade Fon vocabulary also influenced Haitian Creole and the religious languages of Brazil. After French colonization in 1894, French became the sole official and educational language. After independence the government promoted literacy education in indigenous languages, but French remains the main language of national administration and schools.

ranking.name: Akara
ranking.description: Black-eyed peas are soaked and peeled, ground into a paste, seasoned with onion, chili and salt, shaped into small balls and deep-fried; they are crisp outside and soft inside.
ranking.history: Akara is a traditional snack of the Yoruba and Fon of West Africa, and during the Atlantic slave trade it traveled to Brazil with the Africans who were sold, becoming the famous 'acarajé' in Bahia, which is still linked to the rituals of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé. In Benin it is a breakfast and street snack, often eaten with corn porridge or bread. Women in southern Benin sell it in markets and by the roadside, and it is an important source of household income.

ranking.name: Kuli-Kuli
ranking.description: The peanut residue left after pressing peanut oil is mixed with spices, shaped into sticks or rings and fried into a crisp snack with a rich aroma and a very hard texture.
ranking.history: Peanuts are native to South America and were introduced to West Africa by the Portuguese in the 16th century, and are grown in large quantities in the dry north. The peanut residue produced when making peanut oil is not wasted but made into a snack that keeps for a long time, a practice common among the Yoruba, Hausa and Bariba peoples. It is a travel ration and is also often ground and sprinkled on salads or grilled meat as a seasoning.

ranking.name: Wagashi Cheese
ranking.description: A soft cheese made by Fulani herders in the north, who coagulate milk with the juice of the Calotropis leaf; its rind is often dyed red with sorghum stalks, and it can be fried or stewed.
ranking.history: Wagashi cheese is a traditional product of the Fulani (Peul) people, a nomadic people of the West African Sahel who for hundreds of years have driven their herds across the northern grasslands. Without refrigeration, making fresh milk into cheese is a way to preserve dairy, and the coagulant used is the leaf juice of the local plant Calotropis. Today wagashi has gone from being a food of northern herders to an ingredient found nationwide, often sold in the markets of Cotonou.

ranking.name: Red Corn Pâte (Ablo/Wo)
ranking.description: Cornmeal cooked in a red sauce of tomato, onion and palm oil into a corn paste, often served with grilled chicken or fried fish.
ranking.history: Red corn pâte is a traditional dish of the Fon of the south; maize came with Atlantic trade after the 16th century and quickly became the main staple of southern Benin. Coloring the corn paste red with tomato and palm oil is a way of preparing it especially for festivals and religious rituals, and the dish often appears at Vodun ceremonies and family celebrations. It is also one of Benin's most representative festive staples.

ranking.name: Pounded Yam
ranking.description: Boiled yam is pounded repeatedly with a pestle in a wooden mortar into an elastic ball of yam, eaten with peanut soup or vegetable and meat stew.
ranking.history: Yam is one of the oldest staple crops of West Africa, which West Africans have domesticated for thousands of years, and central and northern Benin are part of the West African 'yam belt'. Around August every year many places hold a new yam festival to celebrate the harvest and honor the ancestors. Pounding yam takes a great deal of strength and is traditionally done cooperatively by the women of the household, and the sound of pestle and mortar is an everyday scene of village life.
